content: The United States Public Health Service Commissioned Corps (PHSCC) is a uniformed service of the United States, operating under the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). It is one of the seven uniformed services of the United States and is led by the Surgeon General, who holds the rank of Vice Admiral. The Surgeon General reports directly to the Assistant Secretary for Health (ASH), who may hold the rank of a four-star Admiral. Officers in the PHSCC are considered non-combatants unless directed by the President to serve as part of the armed forces. Members of the PHSCC wear uniforms identical to those of the United States Navy, but with distinct insignia to represent their corps. Their ranks are equivalent to those of naval officers, and they are commissioned through a direct commissioning program. The origins of the PHSCC trace back to the establishment of the Marine Hospital Fund, which was reorganized in 1871 as the Marine Hospital Service. Initially tasked with caring for merchant sailors, the service expanded its mission to address broader public health concerns, including quarantine and disease prevention. Dr. John Maynard Woodworth, a Union Army surgeon, was appointed as the first Supervising Surgeon in 1871. He later became the first Surgeon General of the United States. Dr. Woodworth is credited with formally organizing the Marine Hospital Service into a uniformed service, adopting a military-style structure to create a mobile and adaptable health workforce. He also established professional standards for appointments and designed the service's emblem, featuring a fouled anchor and caduceus. In 1889, President Grover Cleveland signed legislation that officially established the modern Public Health Service Commissioned Corps. Initially, the Corps was open only to physicians, but over the 20th century, it expanded to include other health professionals such as dentists, nurses, pharmacists, environmental engineers, scientists, and more. Today, the PHSCC operates under Title 42 of the U.S. Code and is a key component of the Public Health Service, the primary division of the HHS. The Surgeon General holds a three-star rank (O-9), while the ASH may hold a four-star rank (O-10). The Corps allocates officers to other uniformed services as needed, depending on health and medical requirements. PHSCC officers wear uniforms similar to those of the Navy, with specific insignia to distinguish their affiliation. They receive the same pay and benefits as their military counterparts. Officers are directly commissioned into the Corps, similar to other uniformed services. In certain assignments, PHSCC officers may be detailed to other uniformed services, such as the NOAA Corps or the United States Coast Guard. In these cases, they may wear the uniforms of the service they are assigned to, but with PHSCC insignia. They are also subject to the grooming and appearance standards of the service they are detailed to. The mission of the PHSCC is to protect, promote, and advance the health and safety of the nation. Officers are assigned to various agencies and programs to: Provide healthcare to underserved populations, including American Indians, Alaska Natives, and other groups with special needs. Prevent and control diseases, identify and mitigate environmental health hazards, and promote healthy lifestyles. Improve mental health across the nation. Conduct and support biomedical, behavioral, and health services research, and disseminate findings to health professionals and the public. Collaborate with international agencies to address global health challenges. PHSCC officers are also detailed to other federal agencies, including the Department of Defense, Department of Justice, Department of Homeland Security, and the State Department. Some officers have been deployed to the Middle East and other regions for various assignments. The Corps also provides medical and health professionals to the United States Coast Guard, where they wear Coast Guard uniforms with PHSCC insignia. In recent years, the PHSCC has been actively involved in disaster response and disease prevention. For example, officers played a critical role in identifying and isolating hantavirus in the southwestern United States, providing clinical services to Haitian and Kosovo refugees, and assisting in relief efforts for natural and man-made disasters. Notable deployments include responses to Hurricane Hugo and the Loma Prieta earthquake in 1989, the Northridge earthquake in 1994, and the Oklahoma City bombing in 1995. After the September 11, 2001 attacks, over 1,000 officers were deployed to New York City to provide medical and mental health services to victims and responders. In 2005, following Hurricane Katrina, PHSCC officers established field hospitals and assisted evacuees and responders. The Corps has since implemented a transformation initiative to enhance its disaster response capabilities, including the creation of tiered response teams. Tier 1 teams can respond within 12 hours, Tier 2 teams within 36 hours, and Tier 3 teams within 72 hours. The PHSCC is composed of approximately 6,000 officers across various professional categories, including: Dentists Pharmacists Dietitians Physicians Engineers Scientists Environmental Health Officers Therapists (e.g., physical, occupational, speech, audiology) Health Services (e.g., social workers, physician assistants, optometrists, statisticians, computer scientists, dental hygienists, medical records administrators) Veterinarians Nurses Chiropractors are not currently included in the Corps, although their inclusion is under consideration.
